newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian PM Chernomyrdin to face hostile parliament.
newsitem.headline: Russian PM Chernomyrdin to face hostile parliament.

text.p: Russian Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin faces a hostile State Duma lower house of parliament on Friday to explain a radical government reshuffle which brought youthful reformers into top cabinet positions.

The session coincides with talks in Helsinki between presidents Bill Clinton of the United States and Boris Yeltsin of Russia dominated by Moscow's resistance to NATO's expansion plans -- the only issue on which the Kremlin and the opposition at home are united.

Chernomyrdin, who has turned from an industrial manager into an experienced politician during more than four years in office, tried on Thursday to defuse tensions between the new government and the Duma, dominated by the communists and their allies.
"The government will cooperate with the State Duma in a constructive way," Interfax news agency quoted him as telling leaders of the biggest parliamentary factions.
Chernomyrdin earlier chaired the first meeting of the reshuffled government and praised his two new first deputies, Anatoly Chubais and Boris Nemtsov.
"I'm convinced Anatoly Chubais's expertise, energy and experience will allow us to make colossal progress," he said.
"We need fresh, original, new decisions and, of course, people. And here I am placing a great deal of hope in you, Boris Nemtsov," he told the new first deputy.
Chernomyrdin said there would be more personnel changes in the government but they would not be announced until after Yeltsin's return from Helsinki on Saturday.

He urged his deputies and ministers to work as a single team. "There may be different opinions here at the government meetings but everyone should work as one fist to carry out decisions once they are taken," he said.

Chubais and Nemtsov say they are committed to giving a new push to economic reform by introducing unpopular changes in the paternalistic welfare system and scrapping many benefits granted to enterprises and whole sectors of the economy.
Nemtsov has said the painful changes the new government will have to carry out will make it appear almost "suicidal".
But Chubais said the cabinet's plans would yield visible results quite soon that would help the government, currently very unpopular, to regain support.
The new government's first big challenge will come on March 27, when trade unions plan to hold a national day of protests.
Chernomyrdin has sent top cabinet members to regions where the situation is most tense.

Chubais, visiting the coal-mining region of Kemerovo, said the government was working out "an essentially new policy" but he admitted the graveness of a crisis triggered by a huge backlog in paying wages.
"People really are not getting salaries. It is not an invented problem, it is the most heavy burden for millions and millions," Interfax quoted him as saying.

The Duma invited Chernomyrdin to appear before it to explain the government changes. Despite its loud criticism, it has no power to challenge the reshuffle because the prime minister himself remained in place.
The assembly had been due to debate a non-binding anti-NATO resolution on Thursday declaring that Russia would never become part of the bloc. Deputies held the discussion over until Friday.
They also postponed a planned debate on an emotional call to Yeltsin not to move the mummified corpse of Bolshevik leader Vladimir Lenin from its mausoleum on Moscow's Red Square.
